tldr: We present HOTICE, a reinforcement learning framework that enables humanoid robots to carry payloads through obstacle-cluttered spaces with whole-body coordination without colliding the robot or its payload, demonstrated in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid.
hero_caption: Overall framework of HOTICE. It features decoupled potential fields for the robot and carried object (top left), a dual-agent RL architecture dividing upper- and lower-body actions while preserving whole-body coordination (top right), and a specialist-to-generalist distillation pipeline to deploy a single unified policy to the real robot (bottom).
overview:
For humanoid robots operating in human-centric environments, carrying objects to a destination is an essential capability. However, clutter such as obstacles scattered across the floor, narrow corridors, and low-hanging overhead beams makes this task drastically harder. The robot must not only crouch or step over obstacles to protect its own feet and head, but also carefully adjust its arm positions so the payload does not hit surrounding walls or obstacles.

To address this challenge, the authors developed HOTICE, a whole-body loco-manipulation learning framework. The approach rests on three core ideas. First, it introduces Humanoid-Object Decoupled Potential Fields (HOD-PF), which compute separate spatial potential fields for the robot body and the carried payload. Giving the payload an explicit safety margin allows the robot to proactively lift or retract heavy loads before collisions occur. Second, to overcome the massive action space of whole-body control, it adopts a dual-agent design that learns upper-body (8 arm joints) and lower-body (12 leg joints) control with separate agents. Because both agents share state observations and transportation rewards, the system splits the action space while preserving whole-body balance and carrying performance. Third, it uses a specialist-to-generalist distillation strategy, transferring knowledge from specialized privileged teacher policies trained across diverse individual scenes into a single deployable student policy.

Evaluation was conducted in the MuJoCo simulator and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. The method achieved robust transportation across unseen cluttered scenes and across different payload shapes such as cylinders and spheres, successfully reaching goal locations while avoiding lateral, overhead, and floor-level obstacles.
contributions: Proposed HOD-PF, a decoupled potential field framework that generates separate collision-avoidance guidance vectors for the robot body and the carried object to drive coordinated transportation motions.

Designed a dual-agent reinforcement learning architecture that decouples upper-body (8 arm joints) and lower-body (12 leg joints) control while sharing observations and transportation rewards to efficiently master high-dimensional whole-body coordination.

Distilled specialized policies pretrained across diverse cluttered scenes into a single student policy, achieving strong generalization to unseen scenes and different object shapes alongside zero-shot deployment to a real Unitree G1 humanoid.

sections.heading: Why is carrying objects through cluttered spaces so difficult for humanoids?
sections.summary: Carrying payloads in human-centric cluttered environments pushes fixed arms, wheeled carts, and drones past their limits, making the humanoid morphology advantageous. However, extreme avoidance postures and stable grasping must be coordinated simultaneously under high-dimensional whole-body dynamics and payload mass.
sections.details:
Carrying objects is a cornerstone problem in robotics, critical for delivery, warehouse operations, and domestic assistance. Traditionally, fixed-base manipulator arms, wheeled mobile robots, and drones have been deployed for these jobs. Yet fixed arms have limited reach, wheeled robots struggle with steps and tight passages, and drones face payload weight and flight-space constraints.

Humanoid robots, by contrast, navigate narrow gaps using a human-sized footprint, step over ground obstacles, and duck under overhead beams through flexible whole-body motions. They offer the significant benefit of adapting to diverse environments using a single morphological platform.

Despite this potential, humanoid object transportation in densely cluttered environments has remained largely underexplored. Loco-manipulation—controlling locomotion and manipulation simultaneously—inherently involves a high-dimensional action space that is difficult to learn. Avoiding obstacles further forces the robot into unconventional, extreme poses such as deep crouching and torso twisting. When holding a large, heavy payload, the robot's center of mass shifts dramatically, and the payload itself becomes an extra collision body, severely shrinking navigable free space.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors propose HOTICE (Humanoid Object Transportation In Cluttered Environments). By combining geometry-aware potential field guidance, upper- and lower-body dual-agent decoupling, and policy distillation across numerous environment experts, it achieves robust payload transportation across complex, cluttered environments, including on real hardware.

sections.heading: Where prior work left off: Bridging the gap between traversal and carrying
sections.summary: Legged traversal through tight spaces and humanoid payload carrying have been studied independently, but their intersection—transportation in environments that constrain the entire body—remains largely unexplored. HOTICE bridges this gap by decoupling collision boundaries for the object and the robot.
sections.details:
### II-A Humanoid Traversal in Cluttered Environments
Research on legged traversal through narrow spaces has evolved from classical planning techniques like model predictive control to reinforcement learning. Recently, humanoids have demonstrated parkour maneuvers, rough-terrain locomotion, and contact-aware traversals. Notably, the prior HumanoidPF framework enabled robots to avoid overhead, floor, and lateral obstacles by querying artificial potential fields at keypoints across the body. However, these methods only targeted an unloaded robot. They cannot handle scenarios where a carried payload significantly expands external collision boundaries and drastically alters balance.

### II-B Humanoid Object Transportation
Humanoid object transportation has similarly shifted from trajectory optimization to learning-based methods, achieving robustness against variations in payload mass and size, as well as carrying bulky loads. Recent works increasingly integrate external vision sensors to traverse uneven terrain or execute vision-guided carrying. Nevertheless, most existing studies assume flat, open spaces or sparsely scattered obstacles where the robot can simply take a wide detour. Very few works address realistic human living spaces where obstacles press in from above, below, and the sides simultaneously, requiring the robot and its payload to squeeze through tight margins together.

sections.heading: The setup: Squeezing through obstacles from three directions to reach the goal
sections.summary: In an environment cluttered with lateral, overhead, and ground-level obstacles, a humanoid must transport an object from start to goal without collisions, drops, or falls. While rectangular boxes serve as the primary payload, generalization across varied geometries is also evaluated.
sections.details:
The task setup considered in this work places a humanoid robot in a cluttered scene featuring a combination of lateral obstacles (such as walls and furniture), floor-level obstacles (such as bars and steps), and overhead obstacles (such as hanging beams).

The robot starts at an initial pose $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ already holding target object $\mathscr{O}$, and must transport it to goal position $\mathbf{g} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ without colliding with obstacle set $\mathscr{C}$. The payload $\mathscr{O}$ is primarily a rectangular box, but the framework also accommodates cylinders and spheres, as shown in later experiments. Because this paper focuses on whole-body coordination and obstacle avoidance during transport, episodes begin with the object already grasped; however, to build a complete pipeline, a separate pick-up policy is also trained to lift the object from a table.

Success conditions are strict. An episode is deemed a failure if either the robot body or the payload collides with an obstacle even once, if the payload is dropped, or if the robot falls over. The task is counted as a success only when the robot reaches within tolerance of goal $\mathbf{g}$ while maintaining a secure hold on the object.

captions.F2: Problem formulation and method overview. The humanoid must carry its payload through a constrained passage restricted by obstacles from above, below, and both sides.

sections.heading: Core techniques of HOTICE: Decoupled fields, dual agents, and distillation
sections.summary: HOTICE builds on three main pillars: Humanoid-Object Decoupled Potential Fields (HOD-PF), a dual-agent RL architecture dividing upper- and lower-body control, and a specialist-to-generalist distillation strategy transferring multiple expert policies into a single generalist student.
sections.details:
### IV-A Humanoid-Object Decoupled Potential Fields (HOD-PF)
Extending the earlier HumanoidPF, the authors construct two decoupled potential field channels—one for the robot body and one for the carried object.
- **Standard Guidance Field (SGF)**: For any spatial point $\mathbf{x}$, vector field $\mathbf{F}_{\text{standard}}(\mathbf{x})$ is derived from the negative gradient of attractive field $\mathbf{U}_{\text{att}}$ toward the goal and repulsive field $\mathbf{U}_{\text{rep}}$ away from obstacles. The attractive field uses geodesic distance $\text{D}_{\text{geo}}$, while the repulsive field relies on signed distance function $\text{sdf}(\mathbf{x})$ with influence range $d_0=0.2\,\text{m}$. Querying this field at body keypoints (head, pelvis, feet) yields directional guidance rewards for each link.
- **Object-Centric Guidance Field (OGF)**: An independent vector field $\mathbf{F}_{\text{object}}$ guides the payload and hands. Crucially, this field is computed over inflated obstacles $\mathscr{C}_{\text{inflated}}$ using safety margin $m=8\,\text{cm}$. Carried objects are not directly actuated by joints, making them more vulnerable to control delays and sensor noise, and unlike feet, they cannot simply step over obstacles at the last second. The safety margin induces proactive lifting and tilting behaviors well before nearing an obstacle. Furthermore, the hand reward calculates cosine similarity against hand velocity after subtracting base locomotion velocity component $\mathbf{c}$, isolating and rewarding only the active arm adjustments made for obstacle avoidance.

### IV-B Dual-Agent Learning Architecture
To handle the massive action space of whole-body control, the action space is split into the upper body (8 arm joints) and the lower body (12 leg joints), omitting waist and wrist joints as unnecessary for the task.
Instead of relying on a single monolithic policy, the framework employs two independent Actor-Critic pairs. Both agents receive the same observation state and share termination flags, but output separate actions $\mathbf{a}_{\text{up}} \in \mathbb{R}^8$ and $\mathbf{a}_{\text{low}} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$, which concatenate into a 20-dimensional torque command. Reward functions are also cleanly partitioned: lower-body rewards target walking and balance, upper-body rewards focus on grasp maintenance, and shared rewards govern payload lifting and HOD-PF guidance. This separation prevents gradient conflicts between locomotion and grasping from destabilizing training.

### IV-C Specialist-to-Generalist Distillation
Rather than manually tuning reward weights across distinct scenes, specialized privileged teacher policies are trained in parallel across procedurally generated environments and real-world 3D scans (3D-FRONT). Using DAgger and auxiliary PPO updates, these experts are distilled into a single generalist student policy trained under observation noise and actuation latency.

captions.F3: Comparison between the Standard Guidance Field (SGF, blue arrows) and the Object-Centric Guidance Field (OGF, orange arrows). OGF, computed over obstacles inflated by 8 cm, directs the payload to maintain larger overhead and lateral clearances earlier in the trajectory.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: Superior simulation benchmarks and real G1 navigation
sections.summary: HOTICE outperformed baselines across 20 simulation environments and successfully generalized to 50 unseen scenes as well as cylindrical and spherical payloads. On a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, it safely transported boxes past lateral, overhead, and floor obstacles without dropping them.
sections.details:
### V-A Simulation Experiments
Evaluations in the MuJoCo Playground environment tested boxes up to 3.5 kg and up to 40 cm per side. HOTICE was benchmarked against three ablations: (1) SGF-only (omitting object-specific OGF), (2) a single-agent model (without upper/lower body decoupling), and (3) a model omitting both. Across 20 scenes with 1,000 rollouts each (20,000 total trials), HOTICE achieved substantially higher success rates (SR) and closer final distances to the goal (mDist). In the SGF-only baseline, the payload frequently grazed obstacles; in the single-agent baseline, the robot often fell while trying to step over barriers. In contrast, HOTICE smoothly ducked and lifted the box clear of obstacles.

When testing the policy distilled from 75 expert teachers across 50 completely unseen scenes, it demonstrated strong generalization, posting an average success rate of 80.1% (never dipping below ~70%) and a mean residual distance of 0.27 m. Furthermore, re-anchoring just 8 keypoint locations allowed the policy to transport cylinders and spheres with success rates matching those of rectangular boxes without changing network architecture.

### V-B Real-World Experiments (Unitree G1)
The policy was deployed zero-shot onto a physical Unitree G1 humanoid. The robot ran real-time HOD-PF calculations at 50 Hz using a 2D SLAM map, onboard state estimation, and AprilTag-based tracking of the box pose. Across six trials for each of three obstacle types—lateral, overhead, and floor-level (a rolling pipe)—HOTICE achieved a 6/6 (100%) success rate on lateral obstacles and 5/6 (83.3%) on overhead and floor obstacles. While the SGF-only policy knocked the box against side walls and the single-agent policy lost its balance and fell while stepping over the floor pipe, HOTICE maintained steady, collision-free transport on hardware.

sections.heading: Discussion and limitations: Leveraging contact and dynamic settings
sections.summary: While HOTICE shows outstanding collision avoidance, the authors note several limitations: recovering after accidental collisions, supporting varied carrying poses such as shoulder carries, handling dynamic obstacles, and taking advantage of permissible physical contacts like brushing against walls.
sections.details:
Despite the strong results of HOTICE, the authors outline several clear limitations and directions for future research:

- **Post-Collision Recovery**: Because the policy is optimized specifically to avoid collisions, experiencing a significant impact or external disturbance causes the robot to lose balance without recovery mechanisms.
- **Carrying Style Diversity**: The current policy is restricted to holding payloads in front of the torso with both hands. It does not yet capture more flexible, human-like carrying strategies, such as resting items on the shoulder or tucking them against the hip.
- **Dynamic Obstacles**: The study considers only static obstacles. Extending the framework to open-world environments populated by moving pedestrians and other mobile robots is a necessary next step.
- **Exploiting Permissible Contacts**: Rather than enforcing zero contact everywhere, exploring contact-rich transportation—such as leaning lightly against a wall through tight passages, nudging soft objects like beanbags out of the way, or pushing doors open with the back or legs—presents an exciting avenue.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A step toward practical humanoid payload transportation
sections.summary: HOTICE enables payload transportation in severely cluttered environments by uniting decoupled potential fields, a dual-agent architecture, and teacher-student distillation. The framework provides a solid foundation for future whole-body loco-manipulation research.
sections.details:
This paper presented HOTICE, a whole-body learning framework that allows humanoid robots to transport payloads safely to target destinations through extreme clutter spanning floor, lateral, and overhead obstacles.

Decoupled potential fields (HOD-PF) guide proactive payload avoidance, dual-agent reinforcement learning prevents high-dimensional whole-body control from destabilizing, and multi-teacher distillation grants high generalization and zero-shot real-world deployment capabilities. Validated both in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, this approach represents an important step toward deploying humanoids in logistics, domestic assistance, and other real-world shared spaces.

takeaways: Decoupling potential fields for the robot and its payload with an explicit safety margin (8 cm) naturally induces proactive lifting and avoidance maneuvers for heavy payloads.

In whole-body loco-manipulation, a dual-agent design dividing upper-body (arms) and lower-body (legs) control while sharing observations and core transport rewards effectively mitigates gradient conflict.
Representing carried payloads with a standardized set of 8 keypoints allows the same policy architecture to handle varied shapes, including boxes, cylinders, and spheres.

DAgger distillation from specialized teacher policies trained in diverse cluttered scenes allows a single student policy to generalize well to unseen environments and transfer zero-shot to real hardware.
limitations: Designed strictly for zero-collision avoidance, the framework lacks post-collision balance recovery mechanisms if an unexpected severe impact occurs.
Grasping is constrained to carrying payloads in front of the torso, omitting versatile human strategies like shoulder carrying or hip resting.
The current policy does not support dynamic moving obstacles or contact-tolerant loco-manipulation, such as pushing soft obstacles out of the path.
